title: India Is Listing 'AI-Proof' Jobs and Sectors It Wants to Lead Globally, Goyal Says
excerpt: The Commerce Ministry is mapping professions AI cannot replace — yoga teachers and Ayurveda practitioners among them — and sectors where Indian brands can lead, Piyush Goyal said in Ahmedabad.
body:
• Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal says his ministry is identifying professions that artificial intelligence cannot replace, alongside sectors where Indian brands can take a global lead.
  • Goyal named yoga instructors and Ayurveda practitioners among the roles he called "AI-proof," arguing that work rooted in human care, trust and physical presence cannot be automated.
  • He pointed to Gujarat's GIFT City, with roughly 100,000 direct and indirect jobs, low taxes and dollar-denominated trade, as a model for services exports.
  • For diaspora professionals in AI-exposed white-collar roles, the ministry's list will signal which India-facing skills and services businesses the government intends to promote next.

India's Commerce Ministry is drawing up a list of professions it considers proof against artificial intelligence, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said in Ahmedabad on Friday, as the government looks for sectors where Indian workers and brands can build a lasting global edge rather than compete on work that software can do.

Goyal named yoga instructors and Ayurveda practitioners among the occupations he described as "AI-proof," according to The Hindu. He also cited personal care and home health aides, arguing that services built on human presence, trust and touch will resist automation even as AI systems take over routine cognitive work. Alongside the professions list, the ministry is identifying sectors where Indian brands, rather than foreign ones, can lead global markets.

"We are identifying some sectors in which the Indian brand can take a global lead. We are identifying professions which are AI-proof. Somebody who's teaching you yoga — can there be an AI alternative to it?"

— Piyush Goyal, Commerce and Industry Minister

A services-export pitch built around GIFT City

Goyal tied the exercise to the government's push to sell Indian services to the world, and held up Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City) as the template. The financial hub, he said, now supports close to 100,000 direct and indirect jobs, offers low taxes, employs a large number of women in financial services, and allows businesses to operate in dollars without currency-conversion friction — conditions he contrasted with the United States. He also cast India as a dependable supplier in a world where supply chains have been disrupted, a pitch aimed at countries looking to diversify away from single-source dependence.

The remarks, reported in similar terms by The Economic Times, extend a consistent line from the minister. At the CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam in November 2025, Goyal argued that India's talent pool and its young, aspirational consumers made it the world's most attractive destination for data centres, and earlier this month in Doha he said India was preparing its workforce for an AI-driven economy through large-scale skilling and re-skilling rather than treating the technology as a threat.

Why the list matters

The framing matters because India's services economy — IT, back-office work, finance and professional services — employs millions in precisely the white-collar categories most exposed to generative AI. A government-endorsed map of "AI-proof" work would shape skilling programs, export-promotion spending and the sectors Indian firms are encouraged to build abroad. Wellness is the clearest early bet: yoga and Ayurveda sit inside a global wellness market the government has been promoting through AYUSH visas, dedicated ministries and trade-show diplomacy.

For the diaspora, the practical read is twofold. Professionals in AI-exposed roles who are weighing a move into India-facing work get an early signal of where policy support will concentrate. Entrepreneurs in wellness, personal care and financial services — sectors with a large Indian-American business presence — are looking at the categories New Delhi intends to brand and back internationally.

What to watch

Goyal did not publish the ministry's list or a timeline for it. The test of the exercise will be whether it arrives as a named set of sectors with skilling and export support attached, or remains a talking point. Trade and services data over the next few quarters will also show whether the GIFT City model — dollar books, low taxes, concentrated financial employment — is replicated elsewhere in India.
